screens.title: Identity Management with FreeIPA
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of FreeIPA and why it matters for large Red Hat environments. FreeIPA bundles Kerberos for authentication, an LDAP directory for user and policy storage, integrated DNS and NTP for discovery and time sync, and a built-in Certificate Authority for issuing internal certificates. That combination gives you a single source of truth for identities and policies, making large fleets manageable and auditable. For a practical administrator, FreeIPA reduces ad hoc local accounts, centralizes access control through HBAC rules, and simplifies service trust with CA-issued certificates. A short example: when you enroll a host into the FreeIPA domain, SSSD on that host consults the FreeIPA server for identity and Kerberos tickets, and HBAC rules determine who may access specific services. Throughout the chapter you will see the typical server-install and client-enroll commands, how to create users and groups, and how to author HBAC rules that enforce least privilege. Keep in mind a common misconception: FreeIPA is not just LDAP plus a web UI, it is an integrated stack — Kerberos, DNS, NTP, and CA are all necessary to make authentication and discovery reliable. By the end you will be able to perform a basic install, enroll clients, and manage users and HBAC policies with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical RHCA skills you will demonstrate with FreeIPA. First, you will describe the architecture and core components of FreeIPA: explain the roles of Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, NTP, and the Certificate Authority and how they interoperate. Second, you will perform a basic installation and initial configuration of a FreeIPA server, ensuring FQDN, DNS, and time sync are correct before running the installer. Third, you will enroll Linux clients into an IPA domain using the client installer and SSSD, and verify authentication with Kerberos tickets and home directory creation. Fourth, you will manage users, groups, and host-based access control rules from the command line and the web UI to enforce least privilege. Each objective matters because FreeIPA is an integrated stack: understanding the why behind each component prevents common failures like DNS or clock skew causing authentication outages. A simple example of application is creating a developers group and an HBAC rule that permits SSH to development hosts only. As you progress, think about how these objectives translate into auditability and reduced operational overhead across many RHEL hosts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Focus
screens.narratorSegment: This page reframes the objectives into actionable practice steps. First, when you describe the architecture, tie each component to a failure mode: for example, DNS misconfiguration breaks SRV lookup causing client enrollment to fail. Second, when installing a server, verify a static IP and FQDN first; a concrete step is adding ipa. example. com to /etc/hosts when DNS is not yet configured. Third, client enrollment is practical: run ipa-client-install with --mkhomedir so users get home directories on first login, and verify with ssh to localhost. Fourth, management and HBAC: create a developers group and an HBAC rule that limits SSH to dev servers only; this enforces least privilege. A common misconception is thinking HBAC replaces local sudo rules — HBAC controls access to services and hosts, while sudo governs privilege escalation. Use both when needed. These practice-focused objectives prepare you for the hands-on activity where you will install a server, enroll a client, create a user and group, and validate login as a newly created user.

screens.title: What is FreeIPA?
screens.narratorSegment: FreeIPA is an integrated identity management solution that combines Kerberos for authentication, an LDAP directory for storing users and policies, DNS for service discovery, NTP for clock synchronization, and a Certificate Authority for issuing internal certificates. Define each piece: Kerberos establishes cryptographic tickets so clients authenticate without sending passwords to every service; LDAP provides a searchable directory that stores user records, groups, and policies; DNS publishes SRV records so clients can discover IPA servers automatically; NTP keeps clocks aligned, a requirement for Kerberos validity; the CA issues certificates so services and clients can establish TLS trust internally. A concrete example: when a user logs into a newly enrolled host, the host gets a Kerberos ticket from the KDC, SSSD consults LDAP to fetch group membership, and HBAC rules are evaluated to decide whether the login is permitted. A common misconception is treating FreeIPA as only an LDAP server plus a web UI — in practice it is the coordination of these services that provides a reliable authentication ecosystem. Key takeaway: understanding FreeIPA means knowing not only its components, but the operational dependencies — DNS and time sync are not optional extras. Consider how a missing SRV record or clock drift might cascade into authentication failures.

keyIdea.title: FreeIPA defined
keyIdea.text: An integrated stack — Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, NTP, and CA — providing centralized identity, policy, and trust for Linux/Unix systems.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is FreeIPA?
An integrated identity management platform for Linux that ties authentication, directory, name resolution, time, and certificates together.
Quick Definition
Kerberos + LDAP + DNS + NTP + CA in one cohesive system.
Component cards
Kerberos: secure ticket-based authentication for services and users.
LDAP: the directory store for users, groups, host entries and policies.
DNS & NTP: service discovery and time sync required for reliable authentication.
CA: issues certificates for TLS between clients and services.
Example scenario
User authenticates on a client: the client obtains a Kerberos ticket, SSSD queries LDAP for groups and policies, then HBAC rules permit or deny the service access. If NTP is skewed or DNS SRV records are missing, the process fails.
Key Takeaway

FreeIPA is more than a directory; it is the coordinated services that enforce secure, discoverable authentication across many hosts.

screens.title: FreeIPA server and clients — roles and components
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the server and client roles so you can design a resilient deployment. A FreeIPA server hosts multiple coordinated services: the LDAP directory (389 Directory Server) stores user and host records; the Kerberos KDC issues tickets used for authentication; BIND provides DNS with SRV records so clients can discover services; Chrony provides NTP to keep clocks synchronized; and the Dogtag Certificate System acts as the internal CA for TLS and certificate-based authentication. Clients run SSSD which authenticates users against Kerberos and queries LDAP for identity and group data; SSSD also evaluates HBAC rules pushed or consulted via the directory. In a typical flow a client requests a Kerberos ticket from the KDC, SSSD consults LDAP for policies, and the client uses DNS SRV lookups to find the closest IPA server. A concrete design example is deploying at least two replica IPA servers to achieve high availability; replicas synchronize LDAP and replicate the KDC principals so authentication continues if one server fails. A common misconception is thinking replicas are passive backups — replicas are active peers that serve authentication and directory queries. Key takeaway: design for DNS, time, and multiple servers to avoid single points of failure.

keyIdea.title: Server vs client responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Servers provide KDC, LDAP, DNS, NTP, and CA; clients run SSSD, request tickets, and obey HBAC policies sourced from the directory.

content.html:
Architecture
Server and client roles
FreeIPA Server Components
LDAP (389): directory for users, hosts, groups, and policy.
Kerberos KDC: issues and validates authentication tickets.
DNS (BIND): publishes SRV records for service discovery.
NTP (Chrony): ensures time sync required by Kerberos.
CA (Dogtag): issues internal TLS certificates.
Client Behavior and Flow
Clients run SSSD for single sign-on. Typical flow:
  1. DNS SRV lookup finds IPA server.
  2. Client obtains Kerberos ticket from KDC.
  3. SSSD queries LDAP for user and group attributes.
  4. SSSD evaluates HBAC rules to allow or deny service access.
Common misconception

Replicas are active peers, not passive backups; design for multiple active servers to provide resilience.

screens.title: Preparing a server for ipa-server-install
screens.narratorSegment: Before running ipa-server-install you must prepare the host to avoid common failures. Begin by ensuring the host has a stable static IP and a fully qualified domain name that resolves. If DNS is not yet authoritative, add an /etc/hosts entry for the server's FQDN and static IP to allow the installer to validate names. Install the ipa-server and ipa-server-dns packages and confirm Chrony or another NTP service is running so the system clock is synchronized. Also check that firewall rules or SELinux policies allow the necessary ports for LDAP, Kerberos, HTTP(S), DNS, and the CA — network connectivity is a frequent cause of failed installs. A concrete preflight sequence: set hostname with hostnamectl, verify resolvability, install packages, start and enable chronyd, and open ports or temporarily disable firewalls in a controlled lab environment. One misconception to avoid is assuming the installer will silently fix DNS or time issues — while the installer can configure DNS if requested, it still relies on correct host identity and reachable network services. Key takeaway: invest time in preflight checks; they prevent long, hard-to-diagnose errors during installation.

keyIdea.title: Preflight essentials
keyIdea.text: FQDN, static IP, DNS resolution, and correct time are mandatory prerequisites before running ipa-server-install.

content.html:
Process Flow
Preparing a server for installation
Preflight checklist
  • Set FQDN: sudo hostnamectl set-hostname ipa.example.com
  • Ensure static IP and resolvability (or temporary /etc/hosts entry)
  • Install packages: sudo dnf install -y ipa-server ipa-server-dns
  • Start NTP: enable and start chronyd to avoid Kerberos time issues
  • Verify open ports or allowed firewall rules for LDAP, Kerberos, DNS, HTTP
Why each step matters
DNS and FQDN ensure the installer can register records. NTP alignment is required because Kerberos tickets are time-sensitive. Package installation and port access let the installer provision services like the KDC and DNS. Missing any of these causes interactive failures or misconfigured services.
Common mistake

Skipping time sync or leaving DNS misconfigured is the most common cause of later authentication failures.

screens.title: Running ipa-server-install
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through a canonical ipa-server-install command so you can see what each option accomplishes. The command automates configuration of LDAP, Kerberos, DNS, NTP, and the CA. For example, this common form of the command includes directory manager and admin passwords, the hostname, domain, and realm names, and DNS setup flags. The installer will configure forwarders and reverse zones if requested, create the LDAP suffix, and initialize the Dogtag CA. After the run, create an admin Kerberos ticket with kinit admin to begin managing the server. A concrete example command is shown in the visual pane; notice the flags: --setup-dns instructs the installer to configure BIND, --auto-forwarders and --auto-reverse instruct it to create forward and reverse DNS zones automatically, and -U makes the installer unattended for scripted setups. A common misconception is that unattended mode is for production without review; unattended installs are useful for automation but verify passwords and network settings carefully. Key takeaway: understand each installer flag so automation produces the configuration you expect. keyIdea.title: Installer command explained
keyIdea.text: ipa-server-install configures all integrated services; know the flags to control DNS, realm, and automation for predictable installs.

content.html:
Command Walkthrough
ipa-server-install explained
Typical unattended command
sudo ipa-server-install \
  --ds-pwd="YourDirectoryManagerPassword" \
  --admin-pwd="YourAdminPassword" \
  --hostname=ipa.example.com \
  --domain=example.com \
  --realm=EXAMPLE.COM \
  --setup-dns \
  --auto-forwarders \
  --auto-reverse \
  -U
The installer will provision LDAP, KDC, DNS, NTP integration, and the internal CA. -U runs unattended for automation.
Post-install steps
  • Run kinit admin to obtain a Kerberos ticket for admin tasks.
  • Confirm DNS SRV records exist and resolve from clients.
  • Verify CA is issuing host/service certificates as expected.
Key Takeaway

Carefully review installer flags; automation is powerful but requires correct DNS and password handling.

screens.title: kinit and administrative Kerberos tasks
screens.narratorSegment: After installing FreeIPA, obtain administrative credentials by running kinit admin. This command requests a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket for the admin principal, allowing you to authenticate to the KDC without entering the Directory Manager password repeatedly. The ticket proves your identity to services and lets the ipa command-line tool perform privileged operations. A concrete example: run kinit admin, then run ipa user-add to create a new user without additional password prompts. A common misconception is that kinit creates accounts — it does not; it simply caches authentication credentials for the running session. Another pitfall is forgetting to renew or re-acquire tickets when they expire; Kerberos tickets have limited lifetimes and must be refreshed or reobtained for long-lived automation. When scripting, consider keytabs for host principals where appropriate, but be mindful of keytab security. Key takeaway: kinit admin is the gatekeeper to the admin realm; use it intentionally to manage the server and remember ticket lifetime constraints in automation. kinit and administrative Kerberos tasks means kinit admin obtains a kerberos ticket that authorizes administrative ipa actions without repeatedly exposing passwords.. In practical terms, why you must initialize an admin ticket and how it is used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Admin Kerberos ticket
keyIdea.text: kinit admin obtains a Kerberos ticket that authorizes administrative IPA actions without repeatedly exposing passwords.

content.html:
Definition
kinit and admin tickets
What kinit does
kinit authenticates a principal to the Kerberos KDC and obtains a ticket-granting ticket cached for the session. This ticket allows subsequent authenticated operations without re-entering passwords.
kinit admin
Practical notes
  • Use kinit before running ipa commands to ensure your session is authenticated.
  • Tickets expire; plan renewals or use keytabs for unattended machines.
  • kinit does not create accounts; it authenticates existing principals.
Key Takeaway

kinit admin is required to manage FreeIPA after install; handle ticket lifetimes in any automation.

screens.title: Enrolling a client with ipa-client-install
screens.narratorSegment: Enrolling a client connects the host to the FreeIPA domain so users and policies apply. The ipa-client-install command configures SSSD, Kerberos, and DNS discovery on the client. A common invocation is ipa-client-install --mkhomedir --enable-dns-autodiscovery -p admin_password which ensures user home directories are created on first login and allows the client to find IPA servers via DNS SRV records. After a successful run, use ipa-getkeytab to obtain a host keytab if needed. A concrete pitfall: clients often fail enrollment due to DNS or firewall blocking; if you see resolution errors, check /etc/resolv. conf and test that SRV records for _ldap._tcp and _kerberos._tcp resolve to your IPA server. Another mistake is running enrollment before the server's CA certificate is trusted — ensure the client can retrieve the CA or supply its certificate during install. Key takeaway: verify name resolution and network ports before enrolling clients; when in doubt, test basic DNS lookups and connectivity to the IPA server's ports. Terminal Demo
Enrolling a client
Canonical command
sudo ipa-client-install --mkhomedir --enable-dns-autodiscovery -p admin_password
--mkhomedir ensures home directories are created on first login; --enable-dns-autodiscovery uses SRV records to find IPA servers automatically.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Verify /etc/resolv.conf points to IPA server for DNS resolution.
  • Test: host -t SRV _ldap._tcp.example.com to confirm SRV records.
  • Check firewall allows LDAP, KDC, and HTTP(S) to the IPA server.
  • Ensure CA certificate is accessible to the client during enrollment.
Key Takeaway

Client enrollment depends on resolvability and network access; when enrollment fails, verify DNS SRV records and firewall rules first.

screens.title: Managing users and groups with the ipa tool
screens.narratorSegment: FreeIPA provides the ipa command-line utility and a web UI for identity management. On a server authenticated by an admin ticket, use ipa user-add to create a user, ipa group-add to create a group, and ipa group-add-member to place users into groups. These actions update the LDAP directory and immediately affect SSSD queries on enrolled clients. A concrete command sequence creates devuser, a developers group, and adds the user to that group. For verification, ipa user-find and ipa group-find show directory entries. A common misconception is expecting added users to be immediately able to log in without considering HBAC or home directory creation — ensure the client has mkhomedir enabled or create home directories manually, and ensure HBAC rules do not block the user. Key takeaway: the ipa tool manipulates directory records centrally; changes propagate to clients via SSSD and the next authentication attempt. Managing users and groups with the ipa tool means use ipa user-add, ipa group-add, and ipa group-add-member to manage identities centrally; verify with ipa user-find and group-find.. In practical terms, commands to create, modify, find, and delete identities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Example
User and group management
# Create a user
ipa user-add jsmith --first=John --last=Smith --email=jsmith@example.com

# Modify or delete
ipa user-mod jsmith --setattr=description="Junior Admin"
ipa user-del jsmith

# Group management
ipa group-add developers
ipa group-add-member developers --users=jsmith,asmith
ipa group-find
Notes and verification
These commands modify LDAP entries that SSSD will present to clients during authentication. After adding a user, attempt to SSH to an enrolled client to validate account login and home directory creation.
Key Takeaway

Identity changes via ipa are authoritative and should be planned alongside HBAC and client settings for expected access behavior.

screens.title: Host-Based Access Control (HBAC)
screens.narratorSegment: HBAC is FreeIPA's mechanism to define which users or groups can access which services on specified hosts or hostgroups. HBAC rules are enforced by SSSD on the client at login time, so they act as a centralized authorization layer. To create a rule, add the hbac rule, then specify the subject groups, target hosts or hostgroups, and services such as ssh. For example, create allow_dev_ssh, add the developers group, target dev-server. example. com, add the ssh service, and enable the rule. That sequence ensures only developers may SSH into that host. A common misconception is assuming HBAC replaces local firewall rules or sudo — HBAC controls identity-based access, not network filtering or privilege escalation. Also be careful with using --hosts vs --hostgroups; use hostgroups to apply a rule to many servers at once. Key takeaway: HBAC centralizes access control decisions and enforces least privilege across enrolled clients when correctly composed and enabled. Host-Based Access Control (HBAC) means create hbac rules, add users/groups, add hosts/hostgroups and services, then enable the rule to enforce centralized authorization on clients via sssd.. In practical terms, authoring rules that restrict which users or groups can use services on which hosts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: HBAC enforces access centrally
keyIdea.text: Create HBAC rules, add users/groups, add hosts/hostgroups and services, then enable the rule to enforce centralized authorization on clients via SSSD.

content.html:
Process Flow
Host-Based Access Control (HBAC)
Example HBAC sequence
ipa hbacrule-add allow_dev_ssh
ipa hbacrule-add-user allow_dev_ssh --groups=developers
ipa hbacrule-add-host allow_dev_ssh --hosts=dev-server.example.com
ipa hbacrule-add-service allow_dev_ssh --services=ssh
ipa hbacrule-enable allow_dev_ssh
This sequence binds a subject group to a target host and service, then enables the rule so SSSD enforces it during login.
Notes
HBAC denies by default unless a rule explicitly allows access. Use hostgroups to scale rules across many servers. HBAC is evaluated on the client by SSSD.
Key Takeaway

HBAC rules let you centralize who can access what; design rules to follow least privilege and prefer hostgroups for scale.

screens.title: Integration: DNS, NTP and the Certificate Authority
screens.narratorSegment: FreeIPA's DNS, NTP, and CA are not optional extras — they are foundational to reliable authentication. DNS publishes SRV records that allow clients to locate LDAP and KDC services automatically; if SRV records are missing or incorrect, clients cannot discover the IPA server and enrollment or authentication will fail. NTP synchronizes clocks across servers and clients; Kerberos requires closely aligned clocks because ticket timestamps determine validity. Even small clock drifts can cause authentication failures. The integrated CA issues certificates used by services and clients to establish TLS, ensuring that LDAP, HTTP, and other services are trusted without manual certificate distribution. A concrete example: when you run ipa-server-install with --setup-dns, the installer creates SRV and A records for ipa. example. com; when a client uses DNS autodiscovery during ipa-client-install, it relies on those records. A common misconception is assuming external DNS or third-party CA will replace the integrated services seamlessly; integration reduces configuration overhead but requires careful planning for DNS zones and CA trust. Key takeaway: ensure DNS, time, and CA trust are part of your deployment plan to avoid subtle authentication and service trust issues.

keyIdea.text: DNS, time, and CA services are required for discovery, Kerberos validity, and trusted TLS — treat them as first-class elements of your FreeIPA design.

content.html:
Comparison
DNS vs NTP vs CA
DNS (Discovery)
Publishes SRV and A records so clients can find IPA services automatically. Missing SRV records break enrollment and authentication.
NTP (Time sync)
Keeps clocks aligned. Kerberos tickets are time-sensitive; clock skew leads to authentication failures.
CA (Trust)
Issues internal certificates for TLS and client authentication, simplifying secure communication inside the domain.
Key Takeaway

Treat DNS, NTP, and CA as required infrastructure for FreeIPA; misconfigurations here are the root cause of many authentication issues.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: server, client, user, group, and HBAC
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough ties the earlier concepts together into a repeatable lab. Start on the server: set the hostname and ensure /etc/hosts or DNS resolves ipa. example. com to a static IP. Install ipa-server and ipa-server-dns, then run ipa-server-install with your chosen passwords and DNS flags. After install, run kinit admin to obtain an admin ticket. On the client VM, set its hostname, ensure resolvability to the IPA DNS server, install ipa-client, and run ipa-client-install with --mkhomedir and DNS autodiscovery flags to enroll. Once enrolled, on the server create devuser with ipa user-add and create developers with ipa group-add, then add devuser to the group. Create an HBAC rule to allow only developers to SSH into client systems, then enable the rule. Finally, on the client attempt ssh devuser@localhost and verify the home directory is created and the login succeeds. A common mistake is neglecting DNS configuration; if the client cannot resolve SRV records the enrollment fails. Key takeaway: follow the sequence and verify each step — hostname, package install, kinit, client enrollment, identity creation, HBAC rule, and a login test.

Lab Walkthrough
Hands-on activity steps
Server checklist
  1. Set hostname and confirm resolvability.
  2. Install ipa-server and ipa-server-dns packages.
  3. Run ipa-server-install with DNS flags and strong passwords.
  4. Run kinit admin and confirm admin ticket.
Client and verification

screens.title: Common failures and diagnostic checks
screens.narratorSegment: When clients fail to authenticate, a logical diagnostic sequence often finds the issue quickly. Start with DNS resolution: if you see errors like Could not resolve host ipa. example. com in sssd logs, confirm /etc/resolv. conf points to the IPA DNS server and verify SRV records for LDAP and Kerberos. Next check time: use timedatectl or chronyc sources to ensure clocks are synchronized with the server; Kerberos fails when clocks drift. Then check firewall rules or network connectivity to ensure ports for LDAP, KDC, and HTTP are reachable from clients. Inspect SSSD logs with journalctl -u sssd to see detailed errors; logs commonly show either name resolution failures or Kerberos failures. Another common source is CA trust problems; if the client cannot obtain or trust the CA certificate, TLS connections to LDAP or HTTP may fail. A helpful diagnostic step is running ipa-client-install with verbose logging in a lab to capture the exact failure. Key takeaway: follow DNS → time → network → CA trust → SSSD logs as a repeatable troubleshooting order. This prevents chasing symptoms and accelerates resolution.

Troubleshooting
Common failures and checks
DNS
Verify /etc/resolv.conf and SRV records for _ldap._tcp and _kerberos._tcp.
Time
Ensure NTP/chrony is running and clocks are closely aligned; Kerberos depends on time accuracy.
Network & CA
Check firewall and that the client trusts the server CA certificate for TLS connections.
Logs and commands
Use journalctl -u sssd and klist/kinit to inspect Kerberos tickets. Run ipa-client-install with verbose output in a lab to capture failure details for remediation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of FreeIPA and why it matters for large Red Hat environments. FreeIPA bundles Kerberos for authentication, an LDAP directory for user and policy storage, integrated DNS and NTP for discovery and time sync, and a built-in Certificate Authority for issuing internal certificates. That combination gives you a single source of truth for identities and policies, making large fleets manageable and auditable. For a practical administrator, FreeIPA reduces ad hoc local accounts, centralizes access control through HBAC rules, and simplifies service trust with CA-issued certificates. A short example: when you enroll a host into the FreeIPA domain, SSSD on that host consults the FreeIPA server for identity and Kerberos tickets, and HBAC rules determine who may access specific services. Throughout the chapter you will see the typical server-install and client-enroll commands, how to create users and groups, and how to author HBAC rules that enforce least privilege. Keep in mind a common misconception: FreeIPA is not just LDAP plus a web UI, it is an integrated stack — Kerberos, DNS, NTP, and CA are all necessary to make authentication and discovery reliable. By the end you will be able to perform a basic install, enroll clients, and manage users and HBAC policies with confidence.

These objectives map to practical RHCA skills you will demonstrate with FreeIPA. First, you will describe the architecture and core components of FreeIPA: explain the roles of Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, NTP, and the Certificate Authority and how they interoperate. Second, you will perform a basic installation and initial configuration of a FreeIPA server, ensuring FQDN, DNS, and time sync are correct before running the installer. Third, you will enroll Linux clients into an IPA domain using the client installer and SSSD, and verify authentication with Kerberos tickets and home directory creation. Fourth, you will manage users, groups, and host-based access control rules from the command line and the web UI to enforce least privilege. Each objective matters because FreeIPA is an integrated stack: understanding the why behind each component prevents common failures like DNS or clock skew causing authentication outages. A simple example of application is creating a developers group and an HBAC rule that permits SSH to development hosts only. As you progress, think about how these objectives translate into auditability and reduced operational overhead across many RHEL hosts.

This page reframes the objectives into actionable practice steps. First, when you describe the architecture, tie each component to a failure mode: for example, DNS misconfiguration breaks SRV lookup causing client enrollment to fail. Second, when installing a server, verify a static IP and FQDN first; a concrete step is adding ipa. example. com to /etc/hosts when DNS is not yet configured. Third, client enrollment is practical: run ipa-client-install with --mkhomedir so users get home directories on first login, and verify with ssh to localhost. Fourth, management and HBAC: create a developers group and an HBAC rule that limits SSH to dev servers only; this enforces least privilege. A common misconception is thinking HBAC replaces local sudo rules — HBAC controls access to services and hosts, while sudo governs privilege escalation. Use both when needed. These practice-focused objectives prepare you for the hands-on activity where you will install a server, enroll a client, create a user and group, and validate login as a newly created user.

FreeIPA is an integrated identity management solution that combines Kerberos for authentication, an LDAP directory for storing users and policies, DNS for service discovery, NTP for clock synchronization, and a Certificate Authority for issuing internal certificates. Define each piece: Kerberos establishes cryptographic tickets so clients authenticate without sending passwords to every service; LDAP provides a searchable directory that stores user records, groups, and policies; DNS publishes SRV records so clients can discover IPA servers automatically; NTP keeps clocks aligned, a requirement for Kerberos validity; the CA issues certificates so services and clients can establish TLS trust internally. A concrete example: when a user logs into a newly enrolled host, the host gets a Kerberos ticket from the KDC, SSSD consults LDAP to fetch group membership, and HBAC rules are evaluated to decide whether the login is permitted. A common misconception is treating FreeIPA as only an LDAP server plus a web UI — in practice it is the coordination of these services that provides a reliable authentication ecosystem. Key takeaway: understanding FreeIPA means knowing not only its components, but the operational dependencies — DNS and time sync are not optional extras. Consider how a missing SRV record or clock drift might cascade into authentication failures.

Let's examine the server and client roles so you can design a resilient deployment. A FreeIPA server hosts multiple coordinated services: the LDAP directory (389 Directory Server) stores user and host records; the Kerberos KDC issues tickets used for authentication; BIND provides DNS with SRV records so clients can discover services; Chrony provides NTP to keep clocks synchronized; and the Dogtag Certificate System acts as the internal CA for TLS and certificate-based authentication. Clients run SSSD which authenticates users against Kerberos and queries LDAP for identity and group data; SSSD also evaluates HBAC rules pushed or consulted via the directory. In a typical flow a client requests a Kerberos ticket from the KDC, SSSD consults LDAP for policies, and the client uses DNS SRV lookups to find the closest IPA server. A concrete design example is deploying at least two replica IPA servers to achieve high availability; replicas synchronize LDAP and replicate the KDC principals so authentication continues if one server fails. A common misconception is thinking replicas are passive backups — replicas are active peers that serve authentication and directory queries. Key takeaway: design for DNS, time, and multiple servers to avoid single points of failure.

Before running ipa-server-install you must prepare the host to avoid common failures. Begin by ensuring the host has a stable static IP and a fully qualified domain name that resolves. If DNS is not yet authoritative, add an /etc/hosts entry for the server's FQDN and static IP to allow the installer to validate names. Install the ipa-server and ipa-server-dns packages and confirm Chrony or another NTP service is running so the system clock is synchronized. Also check that firewall rules or SELinux policies allow the necessary ports for LDAP, Kerberos, HTTP(S), DNS, and the CA — network connectivity is a frequent cause of failed installs. A concrete preflight sequence: set hostname with hostnamectl, verify resolvability, install packages, start and enable chronyd, and open ports or temporarily disable firewalls in a controlled lab environment. One misconception to avoid is assuming the installer will silently fix DNS or time issues — while the installer can configure DNS if requested, it still relies on correct host identity and reachable network services. Key takeaway: invest time in preflight checks; they prevent long, hard-to-diagnose errors during installation.

Now we walk through a canonical ipa-server-install command so you can see what each option accomplishes. The command automates configuration of LDAP, Kerberos, DNS, NTP, and the CA. For example, this common form of the command includes directory manager and admin passwords, the hostname, domain, and realm names, and DNS setup flags. The installer will configure forwarders and reverse zones if requested, create the LDAP suffix, and initialize the Dogtag CA. After the run, create an admin Kerberos ticket with kinit admin to begin managing the server. After installing FreeIPA, obtain administrative credentials by running kinit admin. HBAC is FreeIPA's mechanism to define which users or groups can access which services on specified hosts or hostgroups. HBAC rules are enforced by SSSD on the client at login time, so they act as a centralized authorization layer. To create a rule, add the hbac rule, then specify the subject groups, target hosts or hostgroups, and services such as ssh. For example, create allow_dev_ssh, add the developers group, target dev-server. example. com, add the ssh service, and enable the rule. That sequence ensures only developers may SSH into that host. A common misconception is assuming HBAC replaces local firewall rules or sudo — HBAC controls identity-based access, not network filtering or privilege escalation. Also be careful with using --hosts vs --hostgroups; use hostgroups to apply a rule to many servers at once. Key takeaway: HBAC centralizes access control decisions and enforces least privilege across enrolled clients when correctly composed and enabled. FreeIPA's DNS, NTP, and CA are not optional extras — they are foundational to reliable authentication. DNS publishes SRV records that allow clients to locate LDAP and KDC services automatically; if SRV records are missing or incorrect, clients cannot discover the IPA server and enrollment or authentication will fail. NTP synchronizes clocks across servers and clients; Kerberos requires closely aligned clocks because ticket timestamps determine validity. Even small clock drifts can cause authentication failures. The integrated CA issues certificates used by services and clients to establish TLS, ensuring that LDAP, HTTP, and other services are trusted without manual certificate distribution. A concrete example: when you run ipa-server-install with --setup-dns, the installer creates SRV and A records for ipa. example. com; when a client uses DNS autodiscovery during ipa-client-install, it relies on those records. A common misconception is assuming external DNS or third-party CA will replace the integrated services seamlessly; integration reduces configuration overhead but requires careful planning for DNS zones and CA trust. Key takeaway: ensure DNS, time, and CA trust are part of your deployment plan to avoid subtle authentication and service trust issues.

When clients fail to authenticate, a logical diagnostic sequence often finds the issue quickly. Start with DNS resolution: if you see errors like Could not resolve host ipa. example. com in sssd logs, confirm /etc/resolv. conf points to the IPA DNS server and verify SRV records for LDAP and Kerberos. Next check time: use timedatectl or chronyc sources to ensure clocks are synchronized with the server; Kerberos fails when clocks drift. Then check firewall rules or network connectivity to ensure ports for LDAP, KDC, and HTTP are reachable from clients. Inspect SSSD logs with journalctl -u sssd to see detailed errors; logs commonly show either name resolution failures or Kerberos failures. Another common source is CA trust problems; if the client cannot obtain or trust the CA certificate, TLS connections to LDAP or HTTP may fail. A helpful diagnostic step is running ipa-client-install with verbose logging in a lab to capture the exact failure. Key takeaway: follow DNS → time → network → CA trust → SSSD logs as a repeatable troubleshooting order. This prevents chasing symptoms and accelerates resolution.
